title: Bank of Montreal achieves quantum utility amid race to deploy the technology
html:
Canada’s biggest banks have been pouring money into new technologies, including AI and quantum.Andrew Vaughan/The Canadian Press

Bank of Montreal BMO-T has taken a step forward in the race to deploy quantum computing in banking, as the lender says it has demonstrated that the technology can perform work reliably at a more significant scale than traditional computers.

The world’s biggest banks have been investing heavily in developing and commercializing quantum computing, a technology that uses the mechanics of quantum physics to solve complex problems that even supercomputers cannot untangle. BMO says it is the first bank in Canada to achieve “quantum utility” and use the technology for practical applications.

“Quantum utility does not mean that we’re better or smarter or faster than a classical computer yet, but the mere fact we can take a business problem and get a real result out of a quantum machine is probably the first of 10 instances in the world,” BMO chief AI and quantum officer Kristin Milchanowski said in an interview. “To be doing this out of our financial institution is significant.”

BMO developed the capability with Democritus University of Thrace, a public research university in Greece, using International Business Machines Corp.’s (IBM) quantum computers and research team. While BMO is not yet ready to reliably and securely deploy quantum computing in its businesses, IBM expects to launch its first fault-tolerant quantum computer in 2029.

“We still have a few more scientific milestones to go through to where it’s really going to be valuable” to the bank’s businesses, Ms. Milchanowski said.

The bank explored how quantum computing could be used in artificial intelligence models to identify the information that matters most in complex data sets. This could allow the models to find insights with less data than traditional approaches.

This could be used for applications across banking, including more accurate client modelling, improved risk assessment and detection, and more personalized information for clients, according to the bank.

The group focused its work on feature selection, or reducing noise and redundancy in choosing the most important variables from a data set. Ms. Milchanowski compared feature selection to shopping for a sweater and sorting through various options – known as features – such as size, colour and fabric.

In banking, this process could include sorting through credit risk models that commercial bankers use when underwriting loans, or factors that investment bankers consider when pricing an initial public offering.

The bank tested the capability in marketing use cases to help select the most useful features or variables to determine the most appropriate products and services to recommend to a client.

“I felt like there was a place where this type of approach could be novel, and it was worth the 18 months of trial and error to finally get to that point,” Ms. Milchanowski said.

For BMO, the next step is to hit the milestone where a quantum computer can solve a problem faster and with greater accuracy than a regular computer. IBM expects the first demonstrations showing industry impact to come by 2028.

BMO and Canada’s biggest banks have been pouring money into new technologies, including AI and quantum. Banks expect AI to boost productivity and cost savings, and the technology has already started to generate revenue.

In September, the country’s biggest bank, Royal Bank of Canada, created a new role to lead its quantum computing strategy and struck two partnerships with Canadian universities.

The biggest global banks have also been battling to commercialize quantum computing. In 2025, London-based HSBC Holdings Plc said it achieved the world’s first breakthrough in deploying quantum computing for use in financial markets.

Ottawa has been ramping up its efforts to provide financial support for the sector, as the United States, the European Union, Britain and China pledge billions of dollars for quantum computing development.

Some other Canadian companies are experimenting with the technology, such as those in the utilities sector, IBM’s Canada quantum lead Julien Chosson said in an interview. But companies will need to strike partnerships with other organizations to develop quantum responsibly, he said.

“BMO is advanced for a financial institution in the field. They’re already experimenting at utility scale, but it’s also important to accelerate to reach real world applications, to establish strategic partnerships, and [to enable] industry-academia partnerships,” Mr. Chosson said.
summary: It’s the first bank in Canada to use quantum computing for practical applications, BMO says
